name: Papua New Guinea
summary_text: Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Sex between men is criminalised, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the regime of stigma and violence around it applies visibly to transgender people. The Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment of the legal status of sexual and gender minorities across 17 countries in Asia and the Pacific includes Papua New Guinea, with decriminalisation among the topics examined, confirming that the criminal-law position remains a live legal question rather than a settled matter.  Reporting on trans and gender-diverse people in Port Moresby documents direct targeting. ABC News reported in October 2014 that gay and transgender people in the capital are commonly raped or beaten, in some cases by police officers. A 24-year-old gay man recounted being pelted with stones and bottles. Transgender people who present as women face the same exposure to this violence.  One documented pocket of safety exists: Hanuabada, a village built over the sea on Port Moresby's outskirts, where residents live openly and transgender people wear women's clothing in the street without retaliation. This is an exception, not the national pattern.  The wider accountability climate compounds the risk. Human Rights Watch has recorded police abuse, including of children, continuing with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse, and has found that sorcery-related killings in the highlands provinces go largely unpunished, with police routinely taking no action. A visitor who is assaulted has little practical recourse.

name: Poland
summary_text: Detention is the clearest documented threat to a trans visitor in Poland. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and her file recorded a history of violence and sexual assault, meaning she was held in a facility where those risks were live. She was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it.  Trans prisoners have won on the same issue in court. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages, while rejecting the parallel Article 3 claim. The judgment establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and can be won, though it does not prevent the denial from occurring first.  Entry rules are straightforward for short stays: Global Affairs Canada records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, while listing sexual orientation among the reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status. The advisory therefore treats identity-based harassment as an existing condition of travel rather than a remote possibility.  Protection on paper has widened. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, and a March draft amendment to the Penal Code raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence; it passed the Government Legislation Centre in May but the government postponed approval, with a second bill introduced in late October. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. Whether the higher penalties are in force by the time of travel is not settled in these sources.  The wider record shows an official climate that has moved in both directions. HRW's World Report 2025 describes LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as slow and insufficient: in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September the ECtHR ruled that Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum in violation of their rights, calling for a recognition framework. Earlier hostility is documented in statements and enforcement: President Andrzej Duda said in the 2020 election campaign that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism'; municipalities and four voivodeships declared LGBT-free zones after 2015; ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries; and on 7 August 2020 some 47 people were arrested during the Rainbow Night mass arrest, drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman.  Public violence has been recorded at events a visitor might attend. In August 2019 LGBT community members said they felt unsafe amid rising violence, including attacks on the first Equality March in Białystok and a foiled bombing attempt at a march in Lublin. A Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 heard its organiser describe 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' as enemies of Poland.

sources.title: ILGA-Europe 2025 report
sources.documents: Ranks status of LGBTQ rights in Poland as among the worst of EU countries; baseline for overall legal climate.
sources.detail: Cited in article lead as "According to ILGA-Europe's 2025 report" - no URL visible in text

sources.title: Constitution of Poland, Article 18
sources.documents: Defines marriage as union of man and woman under protection of Republic; interpreted by Supreme Court, Constitutional Tribunal and Supreme Administrative Court as limiting marriage to opposite-sex couples and requiring constitutional amendment for same-sex marriage.
sources.detail: Cited as "Article 18 of the Polish Constitution states that 'Marriage, as a union of a man and a woman...'" - no URL visible
